sec.title: Background:
sec.p: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are gaining attention as adjunctive agents in periodontal therapy due to their antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and host-modulatory properties. Their potential adjunctive applications include use as local drug delivery agents, topical pastes, gels or mouthrinses, reinforcements of membranes or implant surfaces, and other applications. While numerous in vitro and animal studies have investigated their utility, the evidence remains scattered, with no comprehensive synthesis available.

sec.title: Objective:
sec.p: This scoping review aimed to map the existing available evidence on AMPs in periodontal therapy, focusing on AMP types, delivery systems, and reported biological, microbiological, and clinical outcomes.

sec.title: Materials and Methods:
sec.p: A systematic literature search was conducted across Medline-PubMed, Cochrane, and Google Scholar for studies published in the past 20 years. Studies were included if they evaluated AMPs for periodontal therapy in vivo or in vitro. The key data extracted included the type of AMP, study model, outcomes, and conclusions. The review followed PRISMA-ScR guidelines.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: A total of 21 studies were included, comprising 13 in vitro studies, 5 animal studies, and 3 clinical studies. The commonly investigated AMP was LL-37. Delivery systems ranged from gels, spays, nanoparticles, and conjugates. Included studies reported significant antimicrobial activity against various periodontal pathogens. Preclinical models and clinical models showed enhanced healing and tissue regeneration. However, variability in experimental design, AMP concentrations, and outcome measures limits comparability across various designs.

sec.title: Conclusion:
sec.p: The existing literature proves AMPs to be a promising therapeutic adjunct in periodontal applications. Clinical data, however, are lacking. Bridging the gap between experimental findings and clinical application requires robust translational research, including well-designed human trials, to evaluate safety, efficacy, and long-term outcomes. This scoping review serves as a foundational reference for guiding future studies toward the clinical integration of AMPs in periodontal therapy.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Periodontal disease is a complex antimicrobial inflammatory disorder, characterized by the formation of plaque biofilm, leading to subsequent periodontal tissue destruction.[1] Based on individual disease susceptibility, the degree of destruction may vary among individuals. At least, 50% of adults exhibit some level of periodontal disease.[23]

The oral cavity harbors numerous microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, viruses, and protozoa. As a complex habitat, the mouth offers several niches – gingival sulcus, tongue, cheek, soft and hard palate, floor of the mouth, throat, saliva, and the teeth for plaque colonization.[4] Of the 700 resident species of the oral cavity, only eight bacterial species have consistently been associated with periodontal disease, including Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Porphyromonas gingivalis, Treponema forsythia, Treponema denticola, Fusobacterium nucleatum, Eubacterium nodatum Prevotella intermedia, and Prevotella nigrescens.[567] The innate immune system plays a principal role in defending these microorganisms. It augments the physical and chemical barriers by producing anti-microbial peptides (AMPs).

AMPs have attracted significant interest as potential adjuncts in the management of periodontal disease due to their dual role in antimicrobial activity and host modulation. While several AMPs have demonstrated promising outcomes in modulating inflammatory responses and suppressing periodontopathogens, most of the available evidence stems from in vitro research and animal models.[89101112131415]

These studies have explored the incorporation of AMPs into various formulations for use as local delivery agents, topical gels, or mouthrinses, all aimed at achieving periodontal health. However, the diversity in experimental setups, AMP types, and outcome measures reported across the literature pose a challenge in synthesizing current knowledge and identifying promising directions for clinical translation.[9161718]

A scoping review is therefore necessary to map the breadth and nature of existing evidence, clarify the current state of preclinical research on local AMP delivery in periodontology and highlight research gaps that must be addressed. By consolidating findings from the available literature, this review will also help guide the design of future translational research to ascertain the potential use of AMPs as viable therapeutic agents in periodontal therapy.

sec.title: MATERIALS AND METHODS
sec.p: This prospective scoping review was conducted in accordance with the original guidance of Arksey and O’Malley[19] and more recent guidelines from Munn et al.[20]

sec.title: Focused question and study eligibility
sec.p: The focused question used for the current literature search was: “What antimicrobial peptides have been utilized for periodontal therapy and what are their reported clinical, microbiological, and biological outcomes?”
The secondary questions were as follows:

list-item.p: What types and formulations of AMPs have been evaluated for periodontal therapy and what delivery systems have been employed?

What specific clinical (e.g., pocket probing depth [PD] and clinical attachment level [CAL]), microbiological (e.g., bacterial load), and biological (e.g., cytokines and matrix metalloproteinases) outcomes have been assessed in studies using AMPs for periodontal therapy?

sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: This scoping review aims to the following:

list-item.p: Identify and summarize the types of AMPs studied for local delivery in periodontal therapy
Describe delivery methods, clinical outcomes, and reported benefits or adverse effects
Map the existing literature and identify the gaps for future research.

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: The inclusion criteria for the studies were as follows:

list-item.p: Trials published in the English language
Randomized controlled trails (RCTs), clinical trials, in vitro assays, and animal or human trials assessing the role of AMPs on periodontal parameters.

sec.p: The exclusion criteria for the studies were as follows:

list-item.p: Pilot studies, reviews, case reports, editorials, communications, or letter to editor.

sec.title: Study search strategy and process
sec.p: A comprehensive search strategy was developed and applied across multiple electronic databases (viz., PubMed/Medline, Embase, Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, ClinicalTrials.gov). The search terms included combinations of: (“periodontitis” OR “periodontal disease”) AND (“antimicrobial peptides” OR “AMPs” OR “LL-37” OR “defensins” OR “nisin”) AND (“local delivery” OR “controlled release” OR “drug delivery” OR “gel” OR “scaffold”).

A manual search of bibliographies of included studies was also conducted. Keywords used were a combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms, which were then employed to adapt to the various databases. The publication period was restricted to the last 20 years with limited to the literature published in English. All articles included for the review were in accordance with the scoping review methodology. Records were collected using reference management software, and the titles were screened for duplicates.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: Two independent reviewers (NP and SH) screened the titles and abstracts based on the preagreed focused question and eligibility criteria. When uncertainty arose, full texts were reviewed to determine eligibility. Disagreements, if any, were resolved through the consensus or consultation with the third and fourth reviewers (AS and GS). Additional manual search was performed of the references from the included full-text articles (NP, SH, and AS). These selected full texts were read for suitability as per the eligibility criteria. The entire process was overseen by AS.

sec.title: Data extraction and outcome of interest
sec.p: Data were extracted independently from the studies and tabulated using Microsoft Excel spreadsheets. The standardized and preagreed data collection sheet included the author title, year of publication, place of study, type and form of AMP used, study design, brief methodology, study results, and conclusion. As this is a scoping review, all studies meeting the eligibility criteria were subject to qualitative research. All reviewers independently verified the collected data.

sec.title: Study selection and data compilation
sec.p: The study selection process is outlined in Figure 1. A total of 636 articles were identified after screening the selected databases. In total, 607 records were excluded after screening for duplicate publications or for the title and abstract not mentioning the relevant MeSH terms. Full-text review and hand searching identified three additional studies for inclusion in the qualitative analysis. Finally, 21 studies were included for this scoping review. The included articles were appraised with key information compiled into a single data table [Table 1 a-c]. Supplementary Table 1 represents the checklist for Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses.

caption.p: Description of included in vitro studies

tr.td: Two groups of bacteria: FAB (S. mutans, S. sanguis, and A. naeslundi); OAB (V. pavrula, P. micra, and F. nucleatum) were grown and maintained on enriched media. Sandblasted Zirconia discs were used for developing biofilms. FAB and OAB were incubated with different concentrations of AMPs. Planktonic growth was established using liquid media

Both AMPs suppressed the planktonic growth of FAB and OAB. The growth inhibition by LL-37 was greater for the OAB than for the FAB. For both AMPs an inhibitory effect obtained on the biofilm was greater with the FAB than OAB. Biofilm formation was inhibited by low LfcinH concentrations, whereas the amount of biofilm mass produced by OAB was barely reduced by LfcinH

The inhibition of planktonic growth and biofilm formation by LL-37 progressed depending on the AMP concentration in two stages: A primary reduction at lower concentrations, LL-37 seems to have an inhibitory threshold concentration for significant reduction of planktonic growth and biofilm mass at higher concentrations, which varied depending on the experimental setup. However, no inhibitory threshold concentration was observed for either bacterial group within the range of the tested LfcinH concentrations

3 systems of chitosan loaded AMPs LL17-32 prepared indigenously P. gingivalis W83 srain was cultured in BHI broth and incubated. Peptide LL17-32 was serially diluted and an equal bacterial suspension was added. Viable counts were quantified by inoculation onto blood agar plates

A significant reduction to approximately 10% of viable counts (as normalized to control) was seen at a concentration of 3.75 µg/mL, this continued in a dose-dependent manner till no colonies were detected at 30 µg/mL. The three kinds of chitosan-coated liposomal LL17-32 systems tested, presented slower and less effective killing activity against P. gingivalis than free chitosans in solution

For the biological studies, peptide LL17-32 and free chitosans all demonstrated strong bactericidal effects against P. gingivalis. The bactericidal activity against P. gingivalis of free LL17-32, chitosan, and chitosan-coated SL liposome when tested in saliva, were all attenuated which may be due to the antibacterial properties of chitosan
Chlorin-e6 conjugated LL-37 loaded nanoemulsion as a nanocarrier for PDT

The combined formulation (Ce6 + LL-37 in nanoemulsion) was tested against multi-species biofilm related to periodontitis as a nanocarrier for PDT The NE incorporated with Ce6 was characterized regarding the physiochemical parameters. Images were obtained by TEM and SEM. Later, the Ce6 and LL-37 incorporated in NE was submitted to UV-Vis analysis and ROS assay

The NE system did not impact the standard UV-VIS spectra of Ce6, and the ROS production was improved while Ce6 was incorporated in the NE. The combination of Ce6 and LL-37 in NE was effective to reduce the viability of all bacteria tested. The treatment with hydrogen-peroxide previous to PDT significantly impacted bacterial viability

Nanoemulsion demonstrated to be an excellent nanocarrier for photodynamic application. - Chlorin-e6 incorporated in nanoemulsion showed great physicochemical and biophotonic parameters. The combination of chlorin-e6 and LL-37 peptide in nanoemulsion is effective to eliminate periodontal pathogenic bacteria

The antibacterial activity of the membranes against S. aureus and E. coli was evaluated by inhibition zone and inhibition ratio assays. Sequential layer-by-layer electrospinning and electrospraying techniques were utilized to prepare a Gln and CS composite GBR membrane containing nHAp and antimicrobial peptide (Pac-525)-loaded PLGA microspheres (AMP at PLGA-MS), which was supposed to have osteogenic and antibacterial activities

A typical morphology of the inhibition zones was observed surrounding the elution solutions of AMP-loaded GBR membranes from various time intervals between 1 week and 4 weeks were loaded. The diameter of the antibacterial ring was measured; the diameter of the positive control group against both E. coli and S. aureus was about 14 mm; in the sample group with 1 week -elution solution, it was 11 and 12 mm against E. coli and S. aureus, respectively; in the sample group with 4-week-elution solution, it was 9 and 11 mm against E. coli and S. aureus, respectively

The Gln/CS composite membrane had an ideal biocompatibility with good cell adhesion, spreading, and proliferation. In addition, the Gln/CS membrane containing nHAp could promote osteogenic differentiation of rBMSCs. According to the in vitro drug release assay and antibacterial experiments, the composite GBR membrane containing AMP-loaded PLGA microspheres had a long-term sustained release of Pac-525, which had bactericidal activity over 1 week and antibacterial activity over a long period of time against two kinds of bacteria, S. aureus and E. coli

In this study, SMAP 28 was linked to affinity- and protein G-purified rabbit IgG antibodies specific to the outer surface of P. gingivalis strain 381 P. micros, A. actinomycetemcomitans, P. gingivalis were cultured for 48 h in enriched media. Each culture was diluted 10-fold. IgG-SMAP28 conjugate was added. At 0, 10, 20, and 30 min, 100 µL were removed and plated on blood agar and incubated. After 9 days bacterial colonies were counted

SMAP28 conjugate when added to an artificially generated microbial community containing P. gingivalis, A. actinomycetemcomitans and P. micros, the antimicrobial activity of the P. gingivalis IgG–SMAP28 conjugate for P. gingivalis was dependent upon the conjugation procedure and the concentration of the conjugate. At 50 g/mL final protein, the conjugate lacked specificity and rapidly killed all three bacteria. At 20 g/mL final protein, the conjugate was more specific and killed P. gingivalis
SMAP28 linked to affinity- and protein G-purified rabbit IgG antibodies could selectively kill P. gingivalis in an artificially generated microbial community

A novel composite coating-containing GO and the AMP Nal-P-113 was coated on smooth titanium surfaces and tested against Gram-positive and Gram-negative microbes in the presence of human gingival fibroblasts

The results showed that Nal-P-113 exhibited a slow and continuous drug release in vitro from the composite coating. The Nal-P-113-loaded GO coating demonstrated excellent antibacterial properties against both Gram-positive S. mutans and Gram-negative P. gingivalis, without no obvious cytotoxicity to HGF cells
The Nal-P-113-loaded GO coating need further optimization for anti-infective and wound healing promoting purpose of peri-implant tissues

A novel antimicrobial peptide, GAPI, has been developed recently by grafting GA to PI. Eight common oral pathogenic bacterial strains were selected for this study. They are S. mutans, S sobrinus, L. acidophilus, L. rhamnosus, A. naeslundii, E. faecalis, P. gingivalis, and A. actinomycetemcomitans All the strains were cultured anaerobically. This laboratory study used minimum inhibitory concentrations and minimum bactericidal concentrations to assess the antimicrobial properties of GAPI against common oral pathogens

The MICs of GAPI against S. mutans and S. sobrinus were 80 µm, whereas the MBCs for these two bacteria were 160 µm and 320 µm, respectively. The MICs and MBCs for A. naeslundii and E. faecalis were 160 µm and 640 µm, respectively. The MICs for P. gingivalis and A. actinomycetemcomitans were 320 µm and 160 µm, respectively. The MBCs for P. gingivalis and A. actinomycetemcomitans were 640 µm and 320 µm, respectively. The results indicated that GAPI showed strong antimicrobial activity of cell membranes, irregular cell shapes, and intrabacterial vacuolisation can be identified. In addition, membrane disruption and leakage of intercellular components were observed

This laboratory study showed that the novel antimicrobial peptide GAPI has promising antibacterial effects against common cariogenic and periodontal pathogens. It can also serve as an alternative to antibiotics in terms of managing dental infection
High affinity HA-binding peptide 1018 (SHABP), the MHABP 1018, and peptide 1018 without additional amino acid sequence (peptide 1018)

Oral multispecies biofilms were grown anaerobically for 3 days. The biofilms were exposed to three peptides at two different concentrations (0.65 and 3.25 µmol/L) for 24, 48, and 72 h. The biofilms were also treated for 3 or 9 min with the peptides (3.25 µmol/L). The percentage of killed biofilm bacteria and biofilm volume was determined by using LIVE/DEAD viability staining and confocal laser scanning microscopy

None of the three peptides, even at a concentration as high as 80 µg/mL, inhibited planktonic growth of dental plaque samples in BHI broth. In the long-term, continuous exposure test, SHABP was superior to MHABP and peptide 1018 in killing biofilm bacteria, especially at high concentration in all experiments. With MHABP and peptide 1018, killing on day 3 was markedly greater than after 24- and 48-h exposure, yet significantly less than with SHABP
The modified peptide 1018 with high HA-binding affinity had higher antimicrobial activity against biofilm microbes and reduced biofilm volume more than the other peptides tested

Active CAMPs were generated by optimized proteolytic cleavage of milk casein. Potential CAMPs sequences were unambiguously determined by unbiased proteome analysis and 301 potential CAMPs were obtained. The activity of four novel CAMPs was tested against S. mutans and P. gingivalis
These natural-safe CAMPs mixtures exhibited high activity in the inhibition of S. mutans and P. gingivalis

Both the active CAMP mixtures and synthetic CAMP standards demonstrated high activity in damaging the bacteria membrane surfaces and inhibiting their growth. CAMPs can induce damage to the cytomembrane of S. mutans and P. gingivalis
The authors examined the inhibitory effects of Nal-P-113 on P. gingivalis W83 biofilms formation. Second, the authors performed gene expression profiling

The results showed that Nal-P 113 exerted its anti-microbial and anti-biofilms effects in P. gingivalis W83 by mediating the energy metabolism, protein synthesis, mobile, and extrachromosomal element functions, transport, and binding proteins of the bacteria. In addition, it was verified that Nal-P-113 acted through the down-regulation of transposase genes or reduction of the miniutilization in P. gingivalis W83 to inhibit the formation of biofilms
In summary, this study provides a molecular biological basis of Nal-P-113 in the prevention and treatment of periodontitis

Human PDLF and GF were cultured from the biopsies of periodontal ligament and gingival tissues, respectively. After cell confluence in 24-well plates, LPS (10 mg/mL) from P. gingivalis, P. intermedia, F. nucleatum, and A. actinomycetemcomitans were added with or without LL-37 (10 mg/mL). After 18 h, the supernatant was collected and analyzed in IL-8 production by the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay

All periodontopathogenic LPS statistically significantly induced IL-8 production in both PDLF and GF (P<0.01) After neutralization with LL-37, both PDLF and GF showed a statistically significant reduction in IL-8 production compared with LPS-treated groups without LL-37 (P<0.01), and the percentage of reduction in IL-8 production in PDLF appeared to be higher than in GF. In addition, the percentage of reduction in IL-8 production varied considerably according to each periodontopathogenic LPS

The antimicrobial peptide LL-37 had an ability to suppress periodontopathogenic LPS-induced IL-8 production in both PDLF and GF. Its LPS-neutralizing activity revealed specificity to periodontopathogenic LPS and seemed to be dependent on the heterogeneity within LPS between different genera
Nisin, melittin, lactoferrin, parasin-1 and LL-37

The activity of the peptides was determined by an agar dilution method under anaerobic and aerobic conditions. The test media contained final peptide concentrations between 0.125 µg/mL and 8 µg/mL (melittin, lactoferrin, parasin-1, LL-37) and between 0.125 µg/mL and 128 µg/mL (nisin) which was tested against numerous periopathogens

Nisin completely inhibited the growth of Megasphaera sp., B. longum, P. micra, A. israelii, A. naeslundii, A. odontolyticus, P. intermedia, S. anginosus, S. constellatus and S. aureus. Melittin and lactoferrin reduced the growth of Megasphaera sp., P. micra, B. longum (melittin) and S. flueggei (lactoferrin). Parasin-1 and LL-37 showed no activity

AMPs, especially nisin and to a smaller degree lactoferrin, might be promising alternatives to antibiotics because of their antimicrobial activity, high resistance to environmental conditions and partially low costs
The MIC and MBC for DP7 were determined via a broth microdilution method. Growth inhibition assays to determine bactericidal effect

Growth inhibition and killing assays confirmed the bactericidal effect of DP7, and treatment with DP7 at MBC eliminated P. gingivalis within 8 h. DP7 had a low cytotoxic effect against human cells. Transmission electron microscopy revealed that DP7 destroyed the bacterial membrane, and confocal laser scanning microscopy revealed its inhibitory effect on P. gingivalis biofilms
DP7, a novel AMP with low mammalian cytotoxicity, inhibits both planktonic and biofilm forms of P. gingivalis by destroying the bacterial membrane and reducing virulence factor gene expression

caption.p: Description of included animal model studies

tr.td: Experimental periodontitis was induced in 81 rats. After disease establishment, animals were assigned to three groups: SRP; SRP + 1PDT, SRP followed by a single PDT session; SRP + 4PDT (n=27), SRP followed by four PDT sessions at 0, 24, 48 and 72 h after SRP. Animals were subjected to euthanasia at 7, 14 and 28 days, and samples were submitted to osteoclast quantification, immunological and microtomography analysis

The animals euthanized after 7 days showed the lowest ratio between bone volume and tissue volume (around 46.5%). For the animals euthanized after 14 and 28 days, all groups demonstrated more than 65% of proportional bone volume presence after 14 days, this result means that all treatments were sufficient to restore periodontal health, but at least 2 weeks were required to restore tissue damage. The quantitative analysis of osteoclast revealed that the number of TRAP-positive cells per mm of alveolar bone surface decreased in the groups treated with a single PDT application (after 14 days) and the groups treated with multiple applications of PDT (after 14 and 28 days), compared with the group treated with the conventional treatment (SRP), after 28 days

Multiple PDT sessions with chlorin-e6 and LL-37 nanoemulsion as an adjunct to scaling and root planning reduced the presence of osteoclast in the local site but did not contribute towards bone regeneration and IL-1β and IL-10 levels

24 Wistar rats were separated into four groups: nicotine-exposed, nonnicotine-exposed, treatment, and control. Rats with periodontitis were given AMP in the gingival line on days 1, 3, and 7 after having their mandibular central incisors ligated for 14 days to induce periodontitis. After AMP treatment, two groups of rats were collected randomly. Each group was decapitated, followed by treatment and histological examination with hematoxylin-eosin staining in the pathology laboratory to view neutrophils and macrophages. The asymmetric Kruskal–Wallis test was used to analyze the data

In mice treated with AMP, neutrophil counts on day 3 were lower than in distilled water (Aquadest) controls. The number of macrophages on day 3 was higher than that of the Aquadest control. Kruskal Wallis test results for neutrophils were P=0.017 and for macrophages P=0.01, where both test results had P<0.05, there were significant differences between the neutrophil and macrophage groups
The administration of AMP effects on decreasing the number of neutrophils and enhancing macrophages in the periodontitis regeneration. In nicotine-exposed rats

Thirty-six five-week-old male SD rats (200–250 g) were subjected to a wire placement around the bilateral maxillary first molars prior infected with bacterial strains. Then the periodontitis rat models were evenly divided into 6 groups: Group A was the positive control (without any antibacterial agent treatment). Group B was washed with sterile water in oral cavity and periodontal pockets. Group C, D, E and F was treated with 1280 µg/mL of Nal-P-113, 2000 µg/mL of penicillin, 80,000 µg/mL of metronidazole and 500 µg/mL of chlorhexidine twice daily for 7 days, respectively. Cytotoxicity to rat gingival mucosa was assessed

At a concentration less than 320 µg/mL which is harmless to normal oral cells, Nal-P-113 can kill bacteria in planktonic state. At a concentration of antimicrobial peptide Nal-P-113 (1280 µg/mL) which only causes slight damages to normal oral cells is needed to kill bacteria in biofilm state. Nal-P-113 eradicated the plaque biofilm more effectively than chlorhexidine

Nal-P-113 exhibits a broad spectrum of bacteriocidal activity and excellent eradicating capability on oral pathogens and their biofilms. Similar to the bactericidal effect of chlorhexidine, Nal-P-113 can inhibit and kill periodontal pathogens in planktonic state and subsequently inhibit their biofilm formation. Moreover, the antimicrobial effect of Nal-P-113 is faster and more potent than penicillin or metronidazole

Reverse phase high-liquid chromatography was used to assess the concentration of Microcin C7 in saliva. The minimum inhibitory concentration and minimum bactericidal concentration of Microcin C7 were analyzed using a broth microdilution method, bacterial growth curve, scanning electron microscopy, and confocal laser microscopy. Effect of Microcin C7 on the expression of inflammatory markers was assessed in rat model

Reverse-phase high-performance liquid chromatography revealed that Microcin C7 could remain 25.5% at 12 h in saliva. At a concentration of <10 mg mL−1, Microcin C7 showed better cytocompatibility, as revealed by a hemolysis test and a subchronic systemic toxicity test. Moreover, the minimum inhibitory concentration and minimum bactericidal concentration of Microcin C7 were analyzed using a broth microdilution method, bacterial growth curve, scanning electron microscopy, and confocal laser microscopy and determined to be 0.16 and 5 mg ml−1, respectively. Finally, in a rat model, 5 mg ml−1 Microcin C7 showed better performance in decreasing the expression of inflammatory factors (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α) and alveolar bone resorption than other concentrations

Microcin C7 demonstrated favorable biocompatibility, antibacterial activity, and anti-inflammatory effect, and could decrease the alveolar bone resorption in a rat model, indicating the promising potential for clinical translation and application on P. gingivalis-associated disease

The antimicrobial activity of nisin and of nisin incorporated in two delivery systems (guar gum biogel and a veterinary toothpaste) were evaluated against a previously characterized collection of canine oral enterococci. Nisin-biogel antimicrobial ability was evaluated in the presence of canine saliva and over a 24-month storage, as well as its safety towards eukaryotic cells

Nisin and nisin-biogel were able to inhibit and eradicate all isolates tested in both planktonic and biofilm forms. Supplemented toothpaste was able to inhibit 95% of the isolates tested. Saliva hampered nisin-biogel activity, but it maintained its antimicrobial activity over the storage period at freezing, cooling and room temperatures. In addition, nisin-biogel showed no cytotoxicity at concentrations up to 200 µg/mL
The results show that nisin-biogel seems to be an appropriate approach for PD control in dogs, being important to test this product in an in vivo controlled clinical trial

fn.p: SRP – Scaling and root planning; PDT – Photodynamic therapy; SD – Sprague Dawley; AMP – Antimicrobial peptides; PD – Probing depth IL – Interleukin-4

tr.td: 51 patients with Stage III GRADE B periodontitis were followed up for 90 days. PPD, CAL and microbial count was assessed at baseline, 7 days, and 90 days

The AMP group (test group) had a reduced PD (periodontal probing depth) and an attachment gain significantly higher than SRP and mino groups (control groups) at day 90. The abundance of periodontal pathogens was decreased in the AMP group at 7 and 90 days compared with the SRP group and Mino group. Only the AMP group showed an increase the abundance of periodontal probiotics including Capnocytophaga, Gemella, and Lactobacillus at 7 and 90 days
AMPs as an adjunct to SRP promote additional clinical and microbiological benefits in the treatment of Stage III Grade B periodontitis

This study was divided into two parts. In Part A, we investigated the user experiences with the P-113 containing oral spray. In part B, 14 subjects in the experimental group used the P-113-containing oral spray, while 14 subjects in the control group used a placebo without the P-113 in a 4-week clinical trial. Participants were asked to use the P-113-containing oral spray or placebo 3 times per day and 5 times per use. Moreover, 3 check-ups and 2 washouts were carried out to evaluate the DMFT score, dental plaque weight, dental plaque index, and gingival index

In part A, up to 91.8% of the subjects in the experimental group were satisfied with the use of the P-113-containing oral spray. In part B, based on our PacBio SMRT sequencing platform and DADA2 analysis, the number of Streptococcus and Porphyromonas in the experimental group was lower than those in the control group. In addition, decreased dental plaque weight, dental plaque index, and gingival index were all observed in the experimental groups
The P-113-containing oral spray has the potential to reduce the dental caries and periodontal disease-related bacteria and to control the dental plaque formation

Double-blinded, randomized clinical study, split mouth in 37 patients with moderate or severe chronic periodontitis. PPD, CAL, BI, were checked at baseline and 7 days after administration of medicine. SEM analyses were conducted to evalaute the plaque structure

The pocket depth and bleeding index values tended to decrease in the experimental group compared with those in the control group. SEM results verified that Nal-P-113 restrained the maturation of plaque. Based on real-time polymerase chain reaction, the levels of F. nucleatum, S. gordonii, T. denticola, and P. gingivalis in subgingival plaque were decreased when the subjects were given Nal-P-113
Nal-P-113 effectively reduces periodontal pathogens and ameliorates periodontal status

tr.td: Identify the report as a scoping review

Provide a structured summary that includes (as applicable): background, objectives, eligibility criteria, sources of evidence, charting methods, results, and conclusions that relate to the review questions and objectives
Describe the rationale for the review in the context of what is already known. Explain why the review questions/objectives lend themselves to a scoping review approach

Provide an explicit statement of the questions and objectives being addressed with reference to their key elements (e.g., population or participants, concepts, and context) or other relevant key elements used to conceptualize the review questions and/or objectives
Indicate whether a review protocol exists; state if and where it can be accessed (e.g., a Web address); and if available, provide registration information, including the registration number
Specify characteristics of the sources of evidence used as eligibility criteria (e.g., years considered, language, and publication status) and provide a rationale

Describe all information sources in the search (e.g., databases with dates of coverage and contact with authors to identify additional sources), as well as the date the most recent search was executed
Present the full electronic search strategy for at least 1 database, including any limits used, such that it could be repeated
State the process for selecting sources of evidence (i.e., screening and eligibility) included in the scoping review

Describe the methods of charting data from the included sources of evidence (e.g., calibrated forms or forms that have been tested by the team before their use, and whether data charting was done independently or in duplicate) and any processes for obtaining and confirming data from investigators
List and define all variables for which data were sought and any assumptions and simplifications made
Critical appraisal of individual sources of evidence§
If done, provide a rationale for conducting a critical appraisal of included sources of evidence; describe the methods used and how this information was used in any data synthesis (if appropriate)
Describe the methods of handling and summarizing the data that were charted
Give numbers of sources of evidence screened, assessed for eligibility, and included in the review, with reasons for exclusions at each stage, ideally using a flow diagram
For each source of evidence, present characteristics for which data were charted and provide the citations
Critical appraisal within sources of evidence
If done, present data on critical appraisal of included sources of evidence (see item 12)
Results of individual sources of evidence
For each included source of evidence, present the relevant data that were charted that relate to the review questions and objectives
Summarize and/or present the charting results as they relate to the review questions and objectives
Summarize the main results (including an overview of concepts, themes, and types of evidence available), link to the review questions and objectives, and consider the relevance to key groups
Discuss the limitations of the scoping review process
Provide a general interpretation of the results with respect to the review questions and objectives, as well as potential implications and/or next steps
Describe the sources of funding for the included sources of evidence, as well as sources of funding for the scoping review. Describe the role of the funders of the scoping review

This is not to be confused with information sources (see first footnote), ‡The frameworks by Arksey and O’Malley (6) and Levac and colleagues (7) and the JBI guidance (4, 5) refer to the process of data extraction in a scoping review as data charting, §The process of systematically examining research evidence to assess its validity, results, and relevance before using it to inform a decision. This term is used for items 12 and 19 instead of “risk of bias” (which is more applicable to systematic reviews of interventions) to include and acknowledge the various sources of evidence that may be used in a scoping review (e.g., quantitative and/or qualitative research, expert opinion, and policy document). sec.title: Location of research
sec.p: The first authors were from various locations, as illustrated in Figure 2. Over half of the published data were originated from China (n = 12), with two studies each from Brazil and Germany and one study each from the UK, USA, Indonesia, Japan, and Portugal. There is strong evidence of international collaboration, with the first and last authors’ affiliations being geographically disparate in several cases.

sec.title: Year of publication
sec.p: Figure 3 illustrates the year in which the studies were published. The earliest publication identified in this review was in the year 2009, followed by a gradual increase in the number of studies thereafter. This trend may reflect emerging evidence of its potential clinical significance and a rising interest within the scientific community.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: All studies included had a periodontal focus; however, the study designs varied significantly [Figure 4]. Most of the studies were in vitro (n = 14), five were animal model, two randomized clinical trials, and one was a split-mouth clinical trial. Patient-related outcomes were reported in three clinical trials.

sec.title: Study characteristics
sec.p: The evidence obtained was derived from heterogeneous sources. A total of 21 studies were included, comprising 13 in vitro studies, 5 animal studies, and 3 clinical studies. The studies varied in their methodological approaches, types of AMPs investigated, and outcome assessed. A summary of study characteristics, including authorship, geographic location, type of AMP used, methodology, results, and funding information, is provided in Table 1a-c. The distribution reflects the broad scope of research in this area, ranging from mechanistic studies to clinical application.

sec.title: In vitro studies (n = 13)
sec.p: The in vitro studies primarily focused on assessing the antimicrobial efficacy, cytotoxicity, and biocompatibility of various AMPs against periodontopathogens such as P. gingivalis, A. actinomycetemcomitans, and F. nucleatum. These studies employed a range of methodologies, including MIC/MBC assays, biofilm inhibition tests, and cell viability assays on human gingival fibroblasts or periodontal ligament cells.

A variety of AMPs were evaluated including LL-37,[891421] Lactoferrin,[8] LL-17-32[9] in conjugated form. Pac-525,[10] SMAP28 conjugate,[11] Nal-P-113,[1222] GAPI,[13] synthetic AMP 1018,[23] casein,[24] and DP7.[15] Most studies reported dose-dependent antimicrobial activity with minimal cytotoxic effects at therapeutic concentrations. The role of various AMPs was tested against numerous putative organisms both Gram-positive and Gram-negative. The organisms were tested in planktonic and biofilm form. A reduction in median growth was noted for the respective organisms. However, there was heterogeneity in peptide formulations, exposure times, and the microbial strain used. Notably, LL-37 was the most commonly studied peptides in this category.
Funding disclosures and conflicts of interest were variably reported. Several studies lacked information regarding funding sources.

sec.title: Animal model studies (n = 5)
sec.p: The five animal studies utilized either a rat (n = 4) or a dog (n = 1) model of experimentally induced periodontitis to evaluate the therapeutic effects of AMPs when locally delivered to periodontal sites. These interventions were often compared with saline or untreated controls. The primary outcomes assessed included histological analysis of inflammation, alterations in alveolar bone parameters, and microbial load reduction.

A variety of AMPs were evaluated including LL-37[18] conjugated nano emulsion, RISE-AP12,[25] Nal-P-113,[26] microcin C7,[27] and nisin.[28] Combination treatment was tested in one study,[18] whereas AMP incorporated in veterinary toothpaste was used in another.[28] Most of the studies demonstrated significant improvement in periodontal parameters in AMP-treated groups compared to controls.

Although the animal studies provided promising translational insights, the limited sample sizes and short follow-up durations were common limitations. Most studies failed to report funding details or conflicts of interest.

sec.title: Clinical trials (n = 3)
sec.p: Only three clinical trials were identified, two of which were RCTs and one was split-mouth clinical trial. These studies investigated the adjunctive use of AMPs such as AMP gel,[17] P-113 in spray form,[29] and Nal-P-113 gel[16] in combination with scaling and root planning.

The outcomes evaluated included PD reduction, CAL gain, bleeding on probing, and microbiological assessments. While all the studies reported favorable clinical improvements, the magnitude of benefit differed. In addition, the trials differed in AMP formulation, dosage, and duration of follow-up. All studies reported relatively short follow-up period (7–90 days).
All clinical trials were performed after obtaining ethical clearance and two disclosed funding sources.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: AMPs are a group of small peptides that exist naturally and play a crucial role in the innate immunity of different organisms.[30] AMPs offer a wide range of inhibitory activity against various microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, viruses, and parasites.[30] These peptides are known to block the inflammatory effects of bacterial toxins.[31] The peptides have co-evolved with oral bacteria and several serve as templates for the development of therapeutic peptides.

Several distinct classes of AMPs, including defensins, cathelicidins, protectins, and histatins, have been extensively characterized in the oral cavity. Upon exposure to periodontopathogenic bacteria, these AMPs exhibit a coordinated and synergistic response, mediating the release of key signaling molecules such as interleukins, chemokines, and cytokines. This cascade facilitates neutrophil chemotaxis to the site of infection and orchestrates a robust and regulated host immune response aimed at maintaining periodontal homeostasis.[32]

Given their dual antimicrobial and immunomodulatory properties, AMPs have emerged as promising candidates for therapeutic application in periodontal disease. However, their clinical translation is challenged by factors such as proteolytic degradation, short half-life, and difficulties in achieving effective concentrations at the target site.[33] Advances in local drug delivery (LDD) systems – including hydrogels, nanoparticles, and bio-adhesive scaffolds – have opened new avenues to overcome these limitations by ensuring sustained peptide release and enhanced stability within the periodontal environment.[34] This has led to an increasing body of research investigating AMP-based local delivery systems as adjuncts to conventional periodontal therapy. Accordingly, this scoping review aimed to map the existing evidence on the LDDs of AMPs as a therapeutic modality in periodontal therapy.

A total of 21 studies were included, comprising 13 in vitro trials, 5 animal model trials, and 3 clinical trials. The findings reveal a growing interest in the use of AMPs due to their broad-spectrum antimicrobial properties, host-modulatory potential, and low propensity for resistance development. However, the distribution of data was skewed toward preclinical data, with limited clinical validation.

In vitro studies constituted the majority (62%) of included literature and predominantly investigated the antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity, and biocompatibility of various AMPs both synthetic and natural against periodontal pathogens. Among the peptides studied, LL-37, in both its natural and conjugated forms, emerged as the most frequently investigated. All studies consistently demonstrated promising antibacterial properties, particularly against biofilm-forming organisms and periodontopathogens.[891011121415182122232435]

Animal studies further supported the therapeutic potential of AMPs. Locally administered AMPs in experimental periodontitis models were associated with reduced inflammation, decreased alveolar bone loss, and significant positive shifts in microbial composition. These findings provide valuable insights, particularly regarding the in vivo behavior of the peptides, their local tissue effect, and response and feasibility of the delivery method.[18252627] One study incorporated AMPs into veterinary toothpaste and assessed the biofilm count in dogs and reported favorable reduction of colony counts.[28] The findings from in vitro and animal models support the biological plausibility and potential mechanisms of action of AMPs. However, limitations such as study design heterogeneity, small sample sizes, short study duration, and species-specific immune responses must be considered when extrapolating these results to human settings.

Despite encouraging preclinical data, clinical evidence remains sparse. Only three clinical studies investigating AMP-based adjunctive therapy were identified, all of which had limited follow-up periods.[161729] While improvements in clinical parameters such as PD and CAL were reported, heterogeneity in study design, peptide type, concentration, and delivery vehicles preclude definitive conclusions. Furthermore, long-term safety, patient-related outcomes, and cost-effectiveness data are lacking.

sec.title: Strengths and limitations
sec.p: A notable strength of the current review is the diversity of AMPs evaluated and the variety of delivery systems explored, including gels, microspheres, nanoparticle-based carriers, and conjugate systems. These approaches may enhance peptide stability, bioavailability, and controlled release for periodontal therapy. However, standardization is lacking in terms of peptide formulations, study designs, and outcome assessments. In addition, the conflict-of-interest statement and the source of funding, which are essential for assessing research transparency and potential biases, were missing in a few studies.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: The use of AMPs represents a promising adjunct to periodontal therapy, with strong support from in vitro and animal model studies. Clinical evidence, however, remains preliminary. Bridging this literature gap requires synchronous efforts through well-designed clinical trials and standardized protocols. With the limited available evidence and with further development and validation, AMPs may offer a novel, targeted approach to managing periodontal infections in an era of rising antimicrobial resistance.

sec.title: Institutional review board statement
sec.p: Ethical review and approval were waived for the study due to its retrospective analytical nature of the study.

sec.title: Conflicts of interest
sec.p: There are no conflicts of interest.
